title: The Bhagavad Gita
description: A dedicated, age-appropriate study of the Bhagavad Gita, the 700-verse dialogue between Arjuna and Krishna within the Mahabharata. Young children meet its setting and simple, universal ideas (doing your best, staying calm, kindness); older learners study its chapters, key concepts, the paths of action, knowledge and devotion, and the rich tradition of commentary and debate. The Gita is presented as a sacred scripture for many Hindus and as a philosophical text studied worldwide; beliefs and interpretations are clearly labelled, and no child is asked to adopt a belief.

structure.title: The eighteen chapters of the Bhagavad Gita
structure.intro: The Bhagavad Gita ("Song of the Lord") appears in the Bhishma Parva of the Mahabharata and contains about 700 verses in 18 chapters. Each chapter is traditionally called a "yoga". Scholars commonly date its composition to roughly the last centuries BCE, though estimates vary. Traditionally, the chapters are often grouped into three sets of six, emphasising action (karma), devotion (bhakti) and knowledge (jnana) respectively — a grouping that commentators interpret in different ways.

sections.name: 1. Arjuna Vishada Yoga
sections.summary: Arjuna's despair: seeing relatives and teachers on both sides, he lays down his bow.

sections.name: 2. Sankhya Yoga
sections.summary: Krishna begins teaching: the eternal self, duty, and the steady-minded person (sthitaprajna).

sections.name: 3. Karma Yoga
sections.summary: The path of action: act without selfish attachment to results.

sections.name: 4. Jnana Karma Sanyasa Yoga
sections.summary: Knowledge and action; Krishna speaks of appearing in every age to restore dharma.

sections.name: 5. Karma Sanyasa Yoga
sections.summary: Renunciation and action compared; inner freedom while acting.

sections.name: 6. Dhyana Yoga
sections.summary: Meditation and mastery of the mind.

sections.name: 7. Jnana Vijnana Yoga
sections.summary: Knowledge of the divine in nature and beyond.

sections.name: 8. Akshara Brahma Yoga
sections.summary: The imperishable; remembrance at the end of life.

sections.name: 9. Raja Vidya Raja Guhya Yoga
sections.summary: The royal knowledge; devotion offered with love — "a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water".

sections.name: 10. Vibhuti Yoga
sections.summary: The divine manifestations in the excellent things of the world.

sections.name: 11. Vishvarupa Darshana Yoga
sections.summary: Arjuna's vision of Krishna's cosmic form.

sections.name: 12. Bhakti Yoga
sections.summary: The path of devotion and the qualities of the devotee.

sections.name: 13. Kshetra Kshetrajna Vibhaga Yoga
sections.summary: The field (body and nature) and the knower of the field.

sections.name: 14. Gunatraya Vibhaga Yoga
sections.summary: The three gunas — sattva, rajas and tamas — qualities of nature.

sections.name: 15. Purushottama Yoga
sections.summary: The supreme person; the image of the upside-down ashvattha tree.

sections.name: 16. Daivasura Sampad Vibhaga Yoga
sections.summary: Divine and demonic qualities in human character.

sections.name: 17. Shraddhatraya Vibhaga Yoga
sections.summary: Three kinds of faith, food, sacrifice and austerity.

sections.name: 18. Moksha Sanyasa Yoga
sections.summary: Liberation through renunciation; summary of the teaching and Arjuna's resolve.

lessons.title: When Arjuna Felt Worried
objectives: Retell that Arjuna felt worried and Krishna helped him
Know it is okay to feel worried and to ask for help
prerequisites: Knows Arjuna and Krishna from the Mahabharata
explanation: In the Mahabharata, before a big battle, the great archer Arjuna sat in his chariot. His friend Krishna was driving it.
Arjuna suddenly felt very worried and sad. He put down his bow and said, "I don't know what to do."

Krishna listened kindly and talked with him for a long time, helping him think clearly. Their conversation is called the Bhagavad Gita. Even strong people feel worried sometimes — and it is good to ask someone we trust for help.

context.text: The Bhagavad Gita is a conversation set in the Mahabharata.
Many Hindus believe Krishna is God and hold the Gita as sacred teaching.

vocabulary.meaning: feeling scared about what might happen

examples: Feeling worried before the first day of school.
Talking to Mama when something is hard.

story.title: Arjuna Puts Down His Bow
story.text: Arjuna looked across the field and felt his hands shake. He sat down in the chariot. Krishna turned around gently. "Tell me what is in your heart," he said. Arjuna told him all his worries. Krishna listened, then began to talk with him calmly. Slowly, Arjuna felt clearer and braver.

speaking: Tell a grown-up about a time you felt worried and who helped you.

lessons.title: Do Your Best, Don't Worry About the Prize
objectives: Explain "do your best and don't only worry about the prize" in simple words
Practise staying calm when things go well or badly
explanation: One famous idea from the Gita is: do your work as well as you can, and don't worry only about the prize or result.
If you are drawing, enjoy drawing carefully instead of worrying about whether you'll win. If you lose a race, you can still be proud of trying hard.
The Gita also talks about staying calm and steady — not too excited when you win and not too sad when you lose.

context.text: This idea is a simplified introduction to teachings found especially in Chapter 2 of the Gita.
Teachers and families explain these ideas in many ways; this is one child-friendly reading.

vocabulary.meaning: feeling good about what you did

examples: Building a block tower carefully even if it might fall.

story.title: The Kite Contest
story.text: At the kite festival, Ivaan worried so much about winning that he couldn't enjoy flying his kite. His grandfather said, "Just fly it as well as you can, and enjoy the wind." Ivaan relaxed and laughed as his kite danced in the sky. He didn't win — but it was the happiest kite flying he had ever done.

lessons.title: Sanjaya's Report
objectives: Explain the setting of the Gita
Describe how the Gita is narrated by Sanjaya
explanation: The Gita takes place at Kurukshetra, just before the great war. Arjuna sees his cousins, uncles and teachers ready to fight against him and does not want to fight them.

The Gita is told in an interesting way: Sanjaya, an adviser to the blind king Dhritarashtra, was given the gift of seeing far-away events. He describes the conversation to the king, so we "hear" it through Sanjaya.
The Gita begins with Dhritarashtra asking, "What did my sons and the sons of Pandu do at Kurukshetra?"

context.text: The narrative frame with Sanjaya is part of the Gita's first chapter.
The Gita forms part of the Bhishma Parva of the Mahabharata.

vocabulary.meaning: someone who gives advice to a leader

examples: Sanjaya describing the battlefield like a reporter.
Arjuna not wanting to fight his teacher Drona.

story.title: The King Who Could Not See
story.text: In the palace, blind King Dhritarashtra sat anxiously. "Sanjaya, what is happening at Kurukshetra?" Sanjaya closed his eyes and, with his special far-seeing gift, began to describe everything: the armies, the conch shells, and Arjuna's chariot between the two sides — and the conversation that was about to begin.

Why didn't Arjuna want to fight?

lessons.title: My Duties
objectives: Explain "duty" with examples from their own life
Relate Arjuna's duty to the idea of responsibility
explanation: A duty is something we are responsible for doing. A student's duty is to learn and try their best. A doctor's duty is to care for patients. A friend's duty is to be kind and loyal.

In the Gita, Krishna reminds Arjuna of his duty as a warrior in that situation. The Gita uses the word svadharma — one's own duty — and says it is better to do your own duty imperfectly than someone else's perfectly.
Doing our duties well, even when they are hard, is a kind of courage.

context.text: The teaching on svadharma appears in Chapters 2, 3 and 18.
Commentators debate how the idea of svadharma relates to social roles; many modern readers emphasise personal responsibility and calling rather than birth-based roles.

vocabulary.meaning: something you are responsible for doing
doing something hard even when afraid

examples: Packing your school bag is your duty.
Feeding a pet is a responsibility.

story.title: The Unfinished Painting
story.text: Zuri was asked to paint the class banner, but she wished she was on the dance team instead. She almost gave up. Her teacher said, "Your job today is the banner. Do it with your whole heart." Zuri painted carefully, and the banner was the best the school had ever had. "My own job, done well," she smiled.

lessons.title: Like a Tortoise
objectives: Describe the qualities of a steady-minded person
Explain the image of the tortoise
explanation: In Chapter 2, Arjuna asks Krishna what a person with a steady mind (sthitaprajna) is like.
Krishna describes someone who is not shaken by sorrow, does not crave pleasure, and is free from fear and anger. Such a person stays balanced in success and failure.
He uses an image: just as a tortoise draws its limbs into its shell, a wise person can draw the senses back from things that distract or disturb them.

context.text: The description of the sthitaprajna is in Bhagavad Gita 2.54–2.72.
Readers relate this ideal to emotional balance and self-regulation; spiritual traditions see it as a step towards liberation.

vocabulary.meaning: sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch

examples: Staying calm after both a win and a loss.
Not getting carried away by a tempting snack.

story.title: Tara the Tortoise's Secret
story.text: When noisy children ran around her pond, Tara the tortoise quietly drew her head and legs into her shell, took a slow breath and waited until it was calm. "I don't run away," she told Kiko, "I just come back to the quiet inside me." Kiko tried closing his eyes and breathing slowly when he felt overwhelmed. It helped.

activities.prompt: A sthitaprajna is a person who…
options: stays steady in joy and sorrow

lessons.title: Not for the Fruit Alone
objectives: Explain the teaching about action and its fruits
Give examples of unselfish action
explanation: A famous verse (2.47) says: you have a right to your action, but not to its fruits (results); don't let results be your only motive, and don't be attached to doing nothing either.
This means doing your work well and sincerely, without being driven only by reward, praise or fear of failure. It does not mean not caring about doing things well!
Acting for the good of others, without expecting something back, is called selfless or unselfish action. Many people, including Gandhi, found this teaching central to their lives.

context.text: Verse 2.47 is among the most quoted verses of the Gita.
Commentators differ on how to understand "not attached to the fruits"; Gandhi called the Gita his "mother" and interpreted it as teaching selfless service.

vocabulary.meaning: caring about others more than yourself

examples: Helping a neighbour carry groceries without expecting a reward.
Studying because you want to learn, not just for marks.

story.title: The Gardener's Mango Trees
story.text: An old gardener planted mango saplings, watered them daily and protected them from goats. "You're old," someone said. "You may never eat these mangoes." The gardener smiled: "I plant because planting is my work, and others will enjoy the fruit." Years later, children climbed those trees and feasted.

lessons.title: Many Paths to One Goal
objectives: Describe karma yoga, jnana yoga and bhakti yoga
Explain that the Gita offers different paths for different people
explanation: In the Gita, "yoga" means a discipline or path, not only physical postures. The Gita describes several paths.

Karma yoga is the path of selfless action. Jnana yoga is the path of knowledge and understanding of one's true self. Bhakti yoga is the path of loving devotion to God. Chapter 6 also teaches dhyana, meditation.

Many commentators say the Gita offers different paths suited to different temperaments, and that they work together rather than competing. Chapter 9 says even a simple offering made with love — "a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water" — is accepted.

context.text: For devotees, these paths lead towards God and liberation (moksha).
Commentators differ on which path the Gita ranks highest; Shankara emphasised knowledge, Ramanuja devotion, and Tilak action.

vocabulary.meaning: in the Gita, a discipline or spiritual path

examples: A nurse serving patients selflessly — karma yoga in daily life, for many readers.
Singing devotional songs — an expression of bhakti.

story.title: Three Friends, Three Paths
story.text: Three friends wanted to live meaningful lives. One volunteered at a hospital, serving tirelessly. One studied philosophy and reflected deeply on who she was. One sang devotional songs every morning with love. When they compared notes, a teacher said, "The Gita describes all three paths. Different people walk different roads up the same mountain."

lessons.title: Sattva, Rajas and Tamas
objectives: Explain the three gunas
Apply the idea of the gunas to everyday choices
explanation: The Gita, drawing on Sankhya philosophy, describes three gunas — qualities that make up nature and influence everything, including our minds.

Sattva is clarity, calm, goodness and harmony. Rajas is energy, activity, passion and restlessness. Tamas is heaviness, inertia, dullness and confusion. Everyone has all three in changing proportions.
Chapter 17 applies the gunas to food, work and faith: for example, fresh, nourishing food is called sattvic. The ideal, according to the Gita, is ultimately to go beyond all three.

context.text: The gunas are discussed in Chapters 14, 17 and 18, drawing on the Sankhya school of Indian philosophy.
Modern readers often use the gunas as a framework for reflecting on habits and moods; it is a philosophical model, not a scientific measurement.

vocabulary.meaning: a quality of nature in Sankhya philosophy

examples: Feeling clear and calm after a good sleep — often called sattvic.
Restlessly switching tasks — rajasic, in this model.

story.title: A Day of Three Moods
story.text: Kavya noticed her day: in the morning, after yoga, she felt calm and clear. At school, she felt restless and competitive, wanting to win every game. By evening, after too much screen time, she felt heavy and sluggish. Her grandmother smiled: "Sattva, rajas and tamas — the Gita says everyone moves between them."

lessons.title: Arjuna's Great Vision
objectives: Describe the vision in Chapter 11
Discuss awe and humility
explanation: In Chapter 10, Krishna describes how the divine is seen in the most excellent things: among mountains, the Himalaya; among rivers, the Ganga; among letters, the first letter "a".

In Chapter 11, Arjuna asks to see Krishna's universal form (vishvarupa). He is given divine sight and sees the whole universe — countless faces, suns and worlds — within Krishna. Arjuna is filled with awe and fear and asks Krishna to return to his familiar form.
For many readers, the vision expresses the vastness of reality and the humility that comes from glimpsing it.

context.text: For devotees, the vishvarupa reveals Krishna as the supreme God containing all existence.
The vision is described in Chapter 11 and has inspired many paintings and sculptures.
Some readers interpret the vision symbolically, as an image of the interconnectedness and vastness of the cosmos.

vocabulary.meaning: wonder mixed with respect or fear

examples: Paintings of the vishvarupa with many heads and arms.
Feeling small and amazed looking at the night sky.

story.title: Under the Stars
story.text: On a camping trip, far from city lights, Ivaan lay on his back and saw thousands of stars and the faint band of the Milky Way. He felt very small and very amazed. His father said, "Arjuna felt something like this in the Gita, but a thousand times more." Ivaan whispered, "Awe."

lessons.title: The Self That Doesn't Change
objectives: Explain the Gita's teaching on the Atman
Distinguish belief from philosophical analysis
prerequisites: Knows the Gita's setting and key ideas
explanation: In Chapter 2, Krishna teaches that the true self (Atman) is eternal: it is not born and does not die. "Weapons cannot cut it, fire cannot burn it."
He uses an image: just as a person takes off worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, the self leaves worn-out bodies and takes on new ones. This relates to the belief in rebirth.
This teaching is central to Hindu belief for many. Philosophers also study it as a claim about personal identity. Students can understand it respectfully whether or not they share the belief.

context.text: Belief in an eternal self (Atman) and rebirth is central to many Hindu traditions; Buddhism, by contrast, teaches anatta (no permanent self).
The verses on the eternal self are in Bhagavad Gita 2.11–2.30.

vocabulary.meaning: in Hindu thought, the true eternal self
the belief that the self is born again in new bodies
what makes someone who they are

examples: The "changing clothes" image (2.22).

story.title: The Clothes Image
story.text: A teacher showed students an old, worn shirt and a new one. "Many readers of the Gita understand verse 2.22 like this," she said, folding away the old shirt. "The person stays the same though the clothes change." One student asked, "Does everyone believe that?" "No," she replied. "Buddhists, atheists and others think differently — and we can understand all these views."

lessons.title: Yoga Is Skill in Action
objectives: Explain nishkama karma, samatva and loka-sangraha
Evaluate how these ideas apply to modern life
explanation: Nishkama karma means action without selfish desire for its fruits. Krishna teaches that inaction is not the answer: one must act, but with the right attitude (Chapter 3).
Samatva, equanimity — treating success and failure, pleasure and pain, alike — is called yoga (2.48). And "yoga is skill in action" (yogah karmasu kaushalam, 2.50).
Krishna also speaks of loka-sangraha — acting for the welfare and stability of the world — saying that the wise should act to set an example for others (3.20–3.25).

context.text: These teachings appear in Chapters 2 and 3.
Thinkers such as Bal Gangadhar Tilak (Gita Rahasya, 1915) emphasised the Gita as a call to action, while others emphasised renunciation or devotion.

vocabulary.meaning: action without selfish desire for results
acting for the welfare of the world

examples: A doctor giving the same care whether or not anyone praises her.
A leader acting as an example for others.

story.title: Tilak's Prison Book
story.text: In 1908, Bal Gangadhar Tilak was imprisoned in Mandalay. In his cell, he wrote "Gita Rahasya", arguing that the Gita's central message was energetic, selfless action in the world. Published in 1915, it inspired many in the freedom movement to see their work as duty performed for others.

lessons.title: Three Great Commentators
objectives: Compare major classical commentaries on the Gita
Explain how commentary shapes interpretation
explanation: The Gita's meaning has been explained in many commentaries (bhashyas). Adi Shankaracharya (traditionally 8th century) read it through Advaita Vedanta: the Atman is identical with Brahman, and liberation comes through knowledge.

Ramanujacharya (11th–12th century), founder of Vishishtadvaita, emphasised devotion (bhakti) and surrender to a personal God, with souls distinct yet inseparable from God. Madhvacharya (13th century), of Dvaita, taught a real distinction between God and souls.

In Maharashtra, the saint Dnyaneshwar wrote the Jnaneshwari (1290), a poetic Marathi commentary that brought the Gita to ordinary people. Different commentaries show how one text can support different philosophies.

context.text: Each commentarial tradition is held as authoritative by its followers.
The Jnaneshwari is traditionally dated to 1290 CE and is a landmark of Marathi literature.
Scholars note that commentators read the Gita in light of their wider philosophical systems.

examples: Shankara's emphasis on knowledge.
Jnaneshwari composed in Marathi ovi verse.

story.title: A Young Saint's Gift
story.text: In 13th-century Maharashtra, the young Dnyaneshwar, said to be only about 16, explained the Gita in beautiful Marathi verse so that people who did not know Sanskrit could understand it. His Jnaneshwari is still sung and studied, and pilgrims to Alandi honour his memory.

lessons.title: A Text That Travelled
objectives: Trace the Gita's global reception
Evaluate modern readings and critical debates
explanation: The first English translation, by Charles Wilkins, appeared in 1785. American writers Ralph Waldo Emerson and Henry David Thoreau admired it. Physicist J. Robert Oppenheimer, who had studied Sanskrit, recalled a verse from Chapter 11 after the first atomic test in 1945.

Gandhi read the Gita daily and interpreted it as an allegory of the inner struggle between good and evil, teaching non-violence — even though its setting is a battlefield. Others, including Tilak and some revolutionaries, read it as justifying righteous action, including struggle.

Critical questions continue: how to reconcile its battlefield setting with non-violence, and how to read verses about varna (social order) — some readers emphasise qualities and action, while critics, including Dr B. R. Ambedkar, argued such verses supported caste hierarchy. Careful study weighs these debates honestly and respectfully.

context.text: Charles Wilkins's translation was published in 1785; Oppenheimer described recalling Chapter 11 in later interviews.
For many Hindus, the Gita is sacred scripture and a daily guide.
Readings of the Gita on violence and on varna differ sharply among commentators, reformers and critics; this lesson presents the debate without settling it.

story.title: Two Readers in One Movement
story.text: During the freedom struggle, one reader of the Gita, Gandhi, found in it a call to non-violent courage. Another, Tilak, found a call to energetic action against injustice. Both were devoted readers, both inspired millions — and both show how a single text can be read in very different ways by sincere people.
